l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: The Sahara appears to the travelers as an immeasurable ocean of sand extending around the Jereed. They observe its heat, blowing sand, salt flats, sparse marshes, rocky hills, and difficult routes where knowledge of hidden wells is essential.

l: date cultivation and trade at Toser, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: Toser’s date gardens are abundantly irrigated, and its dates are considered among the finest. Dates form almost the only food of the inhabitants, their stones cover the streets, and the tribute imposed on the area is equivalent to two bunches from each date-tree.

l: Toser's water system, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: An abundant spring called Meshra rises at a small rocky mountain northwest of Toser. It runs along the city walls, divides into three branches, waters Toser’s gardens and neighboring villages, and eventually disappears into the sand; the town’s wells are insufficient, so inhabitants fetch water from Wad Meshra.

l: Santa Maria, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: Santa Maria returns a horse to the Bey and receives another in exchange, and he is criticized for his delicate feeling and impudence toward the Bey’s officers. He later leaves for Ghabs with an escort of twelve men, although no reliable route to that place is shown on the charts.

l: Sheikh Tahid, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: Sheikh Tahid is imprisoned because he has not prepared the Bey’s tribute. He is repeatedly bastinadoed, including an additional fifty strokes, and is chained after directing searchers to several supposed hiding places where no money is found; he maintains that he cannot pay.

l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: The tribute is collected through a system in which the Sheikh gathers dates from the people and pays the Bey a fixed yearly sum when he arrives. At Toser, the tax is described as equivalent to two bunches of dates for each date-tree, and failure to have it ready leads to imprisonment and punishment.

l: Nefta, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: Nefta, the ancient Negeta, lies about fourteen miles from Toser and is the southern frontier town of the Tunisian territories. It consists of villages separated by gardens, has abundant water, mosques, schools, markets, saints, merchants, landed proprietors, and Shereefs, and serves as an entrepôt called the gate of Tunis for commerce toward the Sahara.

l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: Tunis is the source of commerce sent through Nefta toward the Sahara. It is also associated with the Bey’s authority, with Dutch tiles brought from Tunis appearing in Nefta’s houses, and with a decree placing Jews on the same footing of rights and privileges as other subjects.

l: Sahara mirage, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
s: The travelers repeatedly mistake the Sahara’s salt-covered or sandy surface for water, seeing apparent shores, inlets, bays, and islands. At Nefta and on the return from Toser, the seemingly liquid expanse is identified as the Palus Libya or a salt plain with sand heaps rather than an actual lake.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, and his wife added 1,000 more, after which he was set at liberty. Dates were being harvested in the Jereed, with several varieties described, and their superior ripeness was attributed to only one day of rain during the past year. Moorish feastday entertainment included masked men performing lascivious and indecent actions, which the text presents as a negative aspect of the Moors. Sultan Kaed of the Hammama died at an extremely old age, while Sheikh Ali brought in two loteds after being ordered by the Bey to return with some.

l: Sheikh Tahid, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: His gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, and his wife added 1,000 more. He was then set at liberty.

l: Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died at an extremely old age. During his life he had distinguished himself, including in fighting against the French before Constantina.

l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: The text describes masked men performing revolting, lascivious, and indecent actions during Moorish feastdays. It presents this behavior as the worst side of the character of the Moors.

l: French, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: The text states that Moorish women had never been so profligate as since the arrival of the French in Algeria. Sultan Kaed had also distinguished himself against the French before Constantina.

l: Algeria, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: The arrival of the French in Algeria is associated in the text with increased profligacy among Moorish women.

l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: The Jereed had received only a single day of rain during the past year. The lack of rain was said to have contributed to the superior ripeness of its dates.

l: dates, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Dates were coming in in large quantities and included several kinds, especially Degalah, Trungah, and Monachah. Degalah was described as very sweet and almost transparent; Trungah as plum-shaped and plum-like in taste; and Monachah as larger, drier, mealier, and less sweet. Rain was said to be bad for dates, although the roots of the date tree could not have too much water.

l: loted, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Sheikh Ali brought in two loteds, a female and its young one, which he had shot. The loted was about the size of a fallow deer, with a head like a deer's but with the eye farther up; the female lacked a goat-like beard and instead had long hair extending from the head to the chest and over the fore-legs.

l: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres. His wife added 1,000 piastres, and Sheikh Tahib was set at liberty.

l: date harvest, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: The date harvest was coming in in considerable quantity, though the dates were not in very great abundance. Their superior ripeness was attributed to only one day of rain during the past year in the Jereed.

l: Moorish feastdays, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: On Moorish feastdays, masked men performed lascivious and indecent actions, sometimes dressing as women and dancing indecently. Such actions were described as an indispensable part of the entertainment.

l: death of Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
s: Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died. He was extremely old, and the text remarks that people live to a good old age in the burning climate.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The tourists’ return march to Tunis passed through Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah, amid severe heat, cold, wind, rain, hail, locusts, and heavy losses of men and animals. Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs, and the text records information about Ghabs, Toser, the Jereed, ancient ruins, waterworks, and the tribute collected there. After reaching Tunis, the tourists observed the Bardo, discussed their Boab’s account of marriage and divorce, and received or brought home various Jereed objects and animals. The narrator then describes leaving Mogador aboard the Renshaw schooner and enduring a month-long sea voyage marked by successive gales before reaching England.

l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The party returned toward Tunis and later arrived there, calling at the Bardo to see the guard mounting and hear a military band. Tunisian prices are given for camels, horses, and sheep, and the city is described as a market where a tolerably good horse sells for 800 to 1000 piastres.

l: Ghafsa, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: On the return march, the party reached Ghafsa after experiencing rain, hail, high wind, and severe cold. Ghabs was said to be about 130 miles from Ghafsa.

l: Ghabs, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs after traveling much of the way without seeing anyone. Ghabs was described as having better-built towns than Nefta and Toser, a water-filled river, fertile soil, and dates inferior to those of the Jereed.

l: Toser, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Santa Maria calculated the distance from Ghabs to Toser at 200 miles. The party later marched from Byrlafee, about ninety-one miles from Toser, and dates collected at Toser formed part of the tribute.

l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The Jereed is described as a dry region whose dates are especially good and whose inhabitants supplied tribute in dates, money, woollen goods, blankets, quilts, and animals. The tourists brought home Jereed baskets, dates, woollen articles, skins, and live animals.

l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Before leaving Mogador, the narrator formally took leave of the Governor and received civilities from Moorish authorities and European residents. Merchants in Mogador were closely controlled by the Moorish Government and could not even go aboard vessels to supervise the stowing of their goods.

l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The Bey of the Camp’s exactions on the tribes were suggested as a possible reason for Arabs attacking two couriers. He ordered the party to continue marching after reaching Sidi-Mahammedeah, and he owned Momakeeah and much of the surrounding land. The tourists praised his hospitality and kindness, while the tribute collected during the expedition was associated with his camp.

l: Santa Maria, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs and was described as enterprising and worthy of imitation. He had spent many years in North Africa, spoke Arabic fluently, and planned to visit Tripoli and Ghadames the following season. The party took leave of him when he went to Beja to give an account of his espionage.

l: railways, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The text suggests that railways could be applied to Tunis and notes that the French were already discussing a line from Algiers to Blidah across the Mitidjah. It argues that railways and accompanying water ducts could distribute water across the country and that developed Tunisian resources could make railways profitable.

l: water supply, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The party found bad, salty water at Sheesheeah, brought from some distance. Ancient aqueducts and water-regulating structures were seen at Byrlafee and Gilma, and the text proposes using railway lines and ducts to carry good water from Zazwan to the dry deserts of the Jereed.

l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The tribute was estimated at forty camel-loads of money, six of burnouses, blankets, quilts, and other woollen goods, and 500 camel-loads of dates, for a total of 529 loads. The goods were valued at about £2,860 and the money was estimated at up to £6,250, producing a possible total of £9,110, excluding additional horses, camels, and other animals.

l: return march to Tunis, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The return march involved camps at Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Ben-Habeeba, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah before the party reached Tunis. The march was marked by abrupt changes from intense heat to freezing cold, difficult clay roads, strong winds, locusts, and the deaths or disappearance of many people and animals.

l: deaths from extreme weather, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Two prisoners and one Turk died from excessive heat near Ghortabah. After the temperature suddenly fell, ten men were brought in dead from cold, eight more were buried soon afterward, three were missing, and many camels and horses also perished.

l: sea voyage from Mogador, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: After departing Mogador, the vessel soon lost sight of land and spent the next month at sea. The narrator remained in bed for twenty-five days, living on bread, water, and a little biscuit, while a horse and a young vulture died during the voyage; an aoudad survived and was later lodged in Regent’s Park.

l: gales at sea, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The voyage encountered successive gales of foul wind from the north and northeast, with huge rising waves and foam. The schooner’s bows were repeatedly under water, and Captain Taylor sometimes rushed on deck to swear at the gale and sea.

l: camels, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: Many camels could not reach camp over the clayey ground, and 550 died during the camp’s return. Their prices ranged from 60 to 200 piastres; many good camels were sold for eighty piastres, while one near death sold for one and a half piastres.

l: Renshaw schooner, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
s: The narrator embarked for the Renshaw schooner after taking leave of the Governor at Mogador. The vessel was a beautiful, flat-bottomed, shallow-draft ship built for Barbary ports and carried the narrator, a horse, a young vulture, and an aoudad through severe Atlantic weather.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The unit describes the French bombardment and capture of Mogador in August 1844, during which the Moorish authorities and much of the population fled and wild tribes sacked and burned the city. British and other European residents, who had been detained by Sidi Abdallah Deleero, escaped through great danger with assistance from Mr. Lucas and others. It also records the destruction suffered by the Jews and inhabitants of Mogador and summarizes commerce at Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan, including imports, exports, shipping, and trade restrictions.

Mogador was bombarded by the French on 13 August 1844, and its batteries were silenced after sustained fighting. The Governor and most inhabitants fled, after which wild tribes sacked and burned the city, leaving it largely ruined and unoccupied.

l: French bombardment of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The French bombardment began on 13 August 1844 after the Moors fired twenty-one guns, although the French did not return fire until 2 P.M. The bombardment lasted about twenty-eight hours and caused relatively few French casualties, while the Moors suffered heavily.

l: French bombarding squadron, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The squadron consisted of the ships of the line Gemappes, Suffren, and Triton; the frigate Belle Poule; the steamers Asmodee and Pluton; and some brigs. It silenced the batteries at Mogador before French forces landed on the isle.

The English frigate Warspite reached Mogador on 13 August. Its captain strongly remonstrated with the Moorish authorities but could not obtain permission for the British Consul, his wife, or other Europeans to leave.

l: Mr. Willshire, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The British Consul was detained in Mogador during the bombardment because of his liabilities to the Emperor. He escaped through the sacked city with his wife and others and later reached the Warspite.

l: wife of the British Consul, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The wife of the British Consul was refused permission to leave because Sidi Abdallah Deleero claimed that husband and wife were one. During the escape, she spoke Arabic to a marauding band and persuaded them not to kill her or her companions.

l: Mr. Robertson, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mr. Robertson escaped with his wife and four children during the sack of Mogador. He narrowly avoided a sabre blow and reached the water-port after one of his daughters was threatened with a dagger for money.

l: Mrs. Robertson, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mrs. Robertson escaped with her infant and another child but became separated from Mr. Robertson in the crowd. She later rejoined him at the water-port in a fainting condition.

l: Mr. Lucas, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mr. Lucas constructed a raft from deal planks and cordage and paddled alone to the French brig Canard to seek help. He returned in a boat to rescue the detained fugitives, whose transfer to the Warspite was then arranged.

l: Governor of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Sidi Abdallah Deleero was the Moorish Deputy-Governor in command at Mogador. He refused repeated requests to allow the British and other Europeans to depart before the bombardment.

The Moors opened fire before the French had taken up position and fought effectively for about two hours. After their best gunner, Omar Ei-Haj, was killed, they became dispirited, abandoned the batteries, and fled.

l: Moorish garrison, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The Moorish garrison defended Mogador and the isle but was overcome by the French. About five hundred Moors were reported killed on the isle.

l: wild tribes, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The wild tribes entered Mogador after the Governor and troops fled, sacking, burning, and attacking the inhabitants. They committed murders, assaults, robbery, and other acts of violence against Jews and Europeans.

The Berbers were feared by the escaping Europeans, who believed they might be murdered if discovered. Their attention was chiefly occupied with plundering the city while the fugitives remained near the water-port.

l: Europeans of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The British Consul, his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Robertson, and other Europeans were detained in Mogador during the bombardment. Several escaped through the violence of the sack, aided by Mr. Lucas and others, while some residents were left behind.

l: Jews of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The Jews of Mogador, especially those in the Jewish quarter, were exposed to assault, robbery, stripping, and murder during the sack. Poor Jews were maltreated, and many were left to accompany the natives in misery.

l: Moorish authorities, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The Moorish government, represented locally by the Governor and Deputy-Governor, detained European residents in the hope that their presence might aid the city's defense or lessen the bombardment. Its authorities later fled or failed to prevent the city's destruction.

Morocco supplied Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan with agricultural products and raw materials for export, while receiving manufactured goods and provisions. The text states that Moroccan commerce could expand greatly under a more liberal government and lower duties.

l: isle of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Nine hundred French troops landed on the isle of Mogador on 16 August. After a rough encounter with the garrison, they captured the isle and its forts.

l: Mogador forts and batteries, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The Mogador forts and batteries were subjected to the French squadron's fire and were eventually silenced. The Moorish defenders abandoned them after the death of their best gunner.

l: Mogador water-port, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The Mogador water-port served as the intended place of escape for the Consul's party and the Robertson family. Mr. Lucas reached it by boat after contacting the French fleet, and the fugitives were subsequently rescued from the area.

l: Mogador sack and destruction, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The sack began after the Moorish authorities and population fled, when wild tribes broke into houses, attacked residents, looted goods, and burned property and records. Mogador was left a heap of ruins, with scarcely any house standing entire.

l: escape of the detained Europeans, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: The detained Europeans escaped during the night through streets filled with fighting and plunder. The British Consul's party and the Robertson family endured attacks, while Mr. Lucas secured rescue by rafting to the French fleet.

l: commerce with Morocco, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Commerce with Morocco included British and foreign imports of textiles, metals, dyes, foodstuffs, and manufactured goods in exchange for hides, wool, wax, almonds, fruit, grain, oil, and other produce. The unit gives commercial details for Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan and repeatedly attributes limited trade to high duties, monopolies, and restrictive fiscal laws.

Tangier traded almost exclusively with Gibraltar and maintained active intercourse with that port. In 1856 it imported British goods valued at L101,773 6s. and foreign goods valued at L33,793, while exporting goods to British and foreign ports and sending thousands of cattle and other provisions to Gibraltar.

Gibraltar was Tangier's principal trading partner and received cattle, poultry, eggs, flour, and other provisions. About 3,000 cattle were annually exported to Gibraltar at a fixed duty, with roughly 2,000 more exported at higher rates.

l: Mogador commerce, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mogador exported valuable Moroccan products and imported mainly Manchester cotton goods and other manufactured articles for local and inland consumption. Its trade increased because of strong demand for olive oil, and the text states that more liberal government would greatly expand commerce.

l: Mogador exports, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mogador's exports included almonds, gums, wool, olive oil, seeds, skins, ostrich feathers, and occasionally maize. In 1855 exports were valued at L228,112 3s. 2d. for British ports and L55,965 13s. 1d. for foreign ports.

l: Mogador imports, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
s: Mogador imported Manchester cotton goods, blue salampores, prints, sugar, tea, coffee, iron, steel, spices, drugs, nails, beads, deals, woollen cloth, cotton wool, and mirrors. In 1855 British imports were valued at L136,496 7s. 6d. and foreign imports at L31,222 11s. 5d.

l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, notes
s: The notes discuss the political and religious distinction between the Shereefs and Marabouts, describing the Shereefs as combining regal and sacerdotal authority and the Marabouts as a priestly family. They defend Morocco and the Moors of Barbary against a report of human sacrifice, while recounting the cruelty of Yezeed. The text also describes the peoples, cities, geography, and historical traditions of Barbary, including the Berbers, Algiers, Tunis, Fez, Tangier, the Atlantic System, the Atlas Mountains, and the Sahara.

The Shereefs are described as descendants of the Prophet who combine regal and sacerdotal authority, corresponding to the type of Melchizedek rather than to a strictly priestly order. Because they once possessed the throne, they are said to be jealous of the Marabouts.
The Marabouts are described as a family of priests who have not forgotten that they once ruled Morocco. They are distinguished from the Shereefs, who combine princely and sacerdotal authority.

Abd-el-Kader is described as uniting princely and sacerdotal authority like the Shereefs, although he is not descended from the Prophet. During a storm on his passage from Oran to Toulon, his companions threw handfuls of salt into the sea to appease its fury.

l: human sacrifice, Travels in Morocco, notes
s: The text rejects the report that a beautiful young girl was sacrificed before the Sultan of Morocco, calling it an unmitigated libel. It states that human sacrifice is repudiated by every class in Barbary and is unknown to the Moors.

Tunis is described as containing the hill of Ghamart near Carthage, where a red heifer was sacrificed during a drought. A Bey's frigate returning from Malta also prompted the sacrifice of two sheep to tutelar saints.

Yezeed is described as the son of Sidi-Mohammed and the renegade Irish widow of a sergeant of Sappers and Miners. He is portrayed as a ferocious and cruel tyrant who conducted violent practical jokes, made war widely except on the English, and nevertheless received obeisance from European consuls.

Barbary is described as a region whose inhabitants reject human sacrifice and may sacrifice animals to God or tutelar saints. The notes also discuss its cities, peoples, mountains, deserts, agriculture, and political divisions.

Algiers is included in the middle Western Region and in the mountain system extending across the Barbary States. The Pass of Teniah, leading from Algiers to Mediah, is treated as part of the principal mountain chain in that area.

The Moors of Barbary are described as having no conception of the enormity of sacrificing human beings to God or to a ruler. The notes also discuss competing explanations for the name Moors and criticize an account that portrays them as a uniformly dirty, lazy, inhuman, and indomitable people.

The Berbers are described as comprising numerous tribes and subdivisions, including the Amayeegh, Shelouh, Kabyles, Aoures, Shouwiah, and Touarichs. The text gives traditions about their origins and notes that their present divisions do not correspond exactly to the five ancient principal tribes.

l: Atlantic System, Travels in Morocco, notes
s: The Atlantic System is the name Monsieur Balbi gives to the extensive mountain system of the Maghreb and the elevations scattered through the Sahara. Its principal ridge is said to extend from near Cape Noun on the Atlantic to east of the Great Syrte in Tripoli, with its greatest heights in Morocco.

l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, notes
s: The Atlas Mountains are described as the principal heights of the Barbary region, reaching their greatest elevations in Morocco and diminishing eastward through Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli. Mount Atlas was called Dyris or Derem by ancient and modern aborigines.

The Sahara is described as containing elevations and secondary branches of the mountain system, including branches in southern Tripoli and Libya. Ghafsa is identified as the gate of the Tunisian Sahara, where the sands begin to disappear and the land becomes more suitable for growing corn.

Morocco is described as being ruled by Shereefian princes and as containing the greatest heights of the Atlantic System, especially east of the town of Morocco and southeast of Fez. The text defends its ruler against the allegation that human sacrifice was performed before him.

Tangier is listed among the places in Barbary that have already been described. The notes also state that England might again need to possess its former garrison there if Morocco became an enemy in a European war.

Fez is described as the capital of the realm of that name and as the court of the king in the west. The notes give conflicting traditions about its foundation and suggest that its true history may remain unknown until its library is examined.

This document is a collection of historical reminiscences and accounts centered on St. Paul and Minnesota from territorial and pioneer years through the Civil War and later developments. Its principal subjects are the city’s newspapers and printers, civic institutions, entertainment, fires, transportation, politics, the 1862 Sioux conflict, and Minnesota’s wartime experience. It opens with the growth and rivalry of St. Paul daily papers, the Pioneer, Minnesotian, Times, Press, North Star, and Weekly Journal, covering state-printing patronage, political campaigns, telegraph and Atlantic-cable news, Minnesota’s admission, and Civil War reporting. Printers and editors emerge as important civic and military figures: Capt. E.Y. Shelly and others served in the war, Charles R. Stuart was celebrated for typesetting, and Frank Moore’s career runs from a Minnesotian printer’s “devil” in 1858 to long service with the Pioneer Press. The accounts trace production from early presses to stereotyping and linotype machinery. Other sections portray a growing river city: busy upper-Mississippi steamboat traffic; the Five Million Loan Election and railroad-bond collapse; the Sons of Malta; volunteer fire companies becoming a paid department; destructive hotel and public-building fires; and halls and theaters that hosted music, political meetings, conventions, military activity, fundraisers, and performers including Dan Emmet, the Hutchinson family, Adalina Patti, Frederick Douglass, and James J. Hill. One political satire imagines Robert A. Smith ruling a transformed Mississippi city while the Okons dominate patronage. The Civil War forms the collection’s central crisis. It records printer patriotism, preparations for draft resistance, Minnesota soldiers at Mill Springs and Pittsburg Landing, the First Minnesota battery, Captain William Henry Acker’s death, and public rejoicing at Union successes. On July 4, 1863, while the Pioneer moved offices, the Press alone issued an extra announcing Gettysburg and Vicksburg, helping ignite celebration in St. Paul. The narrative closes the war with St. Paul’s mourning for Abraham Lincoln and its memorial service led by Frederick A. Noble. A major Minnesota emergency is the Great Sioux Outbreak of 1862: attacks at Fort Ridgely, New Ulm, Birch Coulie, and elsewhere; Alexander Ramsey’s emergency response; Henry Hastings Sibley’s campaign; Other Day’s rescue of refugees; Wood Lake and Camp Release; the liberation of captives; convictions and the execution of thirty-eight Indians; Little Crow’s escape and death; and the loss of Sioux lands. A final personal recollection of winning a school spelling match adds a small-scale memory of life before railroads and telegraphs.

James M. Goodhue was a pioneer printer of Minnesota who arrived in St. Paul from Lancaster, Wis., in spring 1849 with a Washington hand press and fonts of type to start a paper in the new territory. He employed Capt. E.Y. Shelly at the Pioneer; they were working together when Goodhue died tragically. He later presented a retrospective account of St. Paul newspaper production, news gathering, conflicts, labor, politics, and wartime experiences.

St. Paul is a Minnesota place that was the capital of the new territory of Minnesota and grew from a busy upper Mississippi steamboat destination into a “great city.” In its early period it had a levee, hotels, stage and steamboat connections, a population of about 10,000, and an active press. Capt. E.Y. Shelly, its first permanently located printer, arrived in 1849; by the 1850s newspapers, printers, editors, and competing Republican and Democratic enterprises made the city a news center. News first came by steamboats and mail coaches and later by telegraph lines. The city celebrated the Atlantic cable in 1858, supported the Five Million Loan by a majority of more than 4,000, and marked Union victories on July 4, 1863 with cheers, cannon, anvils, and firecrackers. Its civic life combined organizations, entertainment, public meetings, and practical services. A Sons of Malta lodge drew men from many occupations. Halls and theaters hosted performances, lectures, drills, political meetings, charitable events, conventions, concerts, and celebrations; a sanitary fair was held in the winter of 1864. Fire protection developed from required marked buckets in 1850 to volunteer companies, hand engines, cisterns, a 1859 parade, and a first steamer in 1866, amid destructive fires including one that destroyed thirty-four buildings in 1860. The central strain is war and loss. During the Sioux outbreak of 1862, St. Paul received refugees, organized home guards, patrolled the bluffs, and feared attack until the Battle of Wood Lake brought safety. Its residents served in the Second Minnesota, followed the battle of Mill Springs anxiously, and later included surviving veterans. The city mourned William Henry Acker through a public reception, funeral, burial, and Acker Post, its first association of Civil War veterans. It also deeply mourned Lincoln’s assassination, draping public and private buildings and holding memorial services. By the later account, it is presented as a transformed great city on the Mississippi River.

St. Paul daily newspapers began as small-staff operations using old hand presses, competing to print speeches, messages, telegraphic reports, and breaking news first. After the Winslow line reached St. Paul, they used telegraph news. They often paused around holidays before expanding late in the Civil War with the city’s population.

Pioneer Press is a daily newspaper that also publishes a Sunday edition. During the war, while the Pioneer was moving its plant, the Press had the field exclusively on July 4, 1863. It delayed an extra until it received the fullest possible details of Union victories, then sold papers to a large waiting crowd. Its Sunday edition illustrates the labor of large nineteenth-century printing, and its composing room later used the Minnesotian proof press. Louis E. Fisher and Richard Bradley served for many years.

The Minnesotian was a St. Paul daily morning newspaper, generally printed the evening before, begun in 1852 by George W. Moore and John P. Owens, its first editor. It was a Republican paper and received the 1857 state-printing contract for the Republican constitutional body, printing that convention’s proceedings. Competitive in news and printing, it bought the first Hoe press brought to Minnesota, published an early illustrated local feature, sought the state-printer position after the 1859 election, and was once misled by bogus telegraphic reports circulated by the Pioneer. Moore was part owner and manager in 1858; Dr. Thomas Foster later controlled and edited the paper after Moore sold his interest in 1860. Foster’s bitter rivalry with Thomas M. Newson’s Times led to a temporary Minnesotian and Times consolidation, followed by Foster’s resumed control. The paper opposed the Five Million Loan measure and attacked Gov. Sibley and railroad bonds. After facing the St. Paul Daily Press and Foster’s sale of the plant, it was absorbed by the Pioneer Press in 1861, becoming part of the present Pioneer Press.

The Pioneer was a daily newspaper, the first paper printed in St. Paul and a leading Minnesota paper in 1857. Under its constitutional-convention contract, it printed Democratic body proceedings. It competed with the Minnesotian and Times for political and telegraphic news, secretly gained telegraph service, briefly held a news monopoly, published Minnesota admission news first in 1858, and later deceived the Minnesotian with fabricated dispatches. It employed editors, printers, and compositors including James Mills, Louis E. Fisher, George W. Armstrong, Marshall Robinson, and editor-in-chief Earle S. Goodrich. On July 4, 1863, it moved to Third and Robert and could not issue an extra on Union victories. It united with Press in 1874.

Times was a St. Paul daily, morning Republican paper and one of three competing papers. It competed with the Pioneer and Minnesotian for presidential messages, telegraphic news, and, after the 1859 election, state printer; it also printed and circulated bogus Minnesotian reports before learning of the deception. Managed by Thomas M. Newson, it traded insults with Dr. Foster of the Minnesotian, briefly merged as the Minnesotian and Times, then dissolved. Newson leased its office and material to W. R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter, who started the St. Paul Daily Press. Its job department employed Richard Bradley and reporter Jebb.

George W. Moore was a printer who came to St. Paul in 1850 and briefly served as foreman of the Pioneer office. He became part owner and manager of the Daily Minnesotian, publishing it with John P. Owens until selling his interest to Dr. Foster in 1860. Appointed collector of the port of St. Paul by Abraham Lincoln in 1861, he held that post for more than twenty years. He was Frank Moore's brother.

Minnesota began as a territory in 1849, a new place that received James Mills and drew young printers and editors; James M. Goodhue established a newspaper there, and Capt. E. Y. Shelly became the first printer to locate permanently. It held a 1857 election for delegates to a constitutional convention, held that convention in preparation for statehood, and entered the Union through a congressional bill; news of admission reached St. Paul by passenger boat in 1858 because telegraphic communication with Washington was lacking. Railroad aid authorized through the Five Million Loan amendment brought grading of nearly 250 miles of road, but company defaults compromised its credit until, under Gov. Pillsbury, it settled by paying half the securities' nominal value. During the Civil War it furnished regiments, including the Second Minnesota Infantry, whose volunteers exceeded the first regiment's quota and whose Mill Springs service was praised. While men were recruited, the Sioux outbreak of 1862 depopulated areas and left thousands homeless, prompting legislative relief and defense. It opposed troop removal, executed thirty-eight Dakota prisoners amid opposition to pardons, and later conducted a draft in counties behind quota.
The 1857 Minnesota election chose delegates; after a close result, Republicans and Democrats held separate constitutional conventions, with proceedings printed under contract.

The Republican Party held a separate constitutional convention in 1857, with proceedings assigned to the Minnesotian. In 1859 it campaigned for Alexander Ramsey and its legislative ticket, using speakers Galusha A. Grow and Schuyler Colfax. After winning a legislative majority, its newspapers, the Minnesotian and Times, disputed state printing patronage before leaders arranged a temporary consolidation. Its first state convention after Minnesota entered the Union nominated Col. Aldrich and William Windom for Congress; Republicans also backed Col. Marshall and attended Frederick Douglass's lecture.

hold Democratic body [as a separate constitutional convention] Democrats held a separate constitutional convention in 1857, and the Pioneer received the contract to print its proceedings. Minnesota Democrats later hoped that Stephen A. Douglas would be nominated for president at the Charleston convention.

James J. Hill participated at the Athenaeum in a mock reenactment of the Heenan and Sayers prize fight, assigned to imitate Sayers; after Theodore Borup made a false pass, Hill knocked him out rather than follow the planned result.
A grand river, called the Father of Water, stretches from the North Star State to the Gulf of Mexico, following an unmolested course toward the boundless ocean as surrounding city greatly changes.

Henry Hastings Sibley is a governor of Minnesota during the bond dispute and later a military commander. As Gov. Sibley, he initially refused to issue railroad bonds until the state's rights were protected, but, following the attorney general's advice and the supreme court's mandate, reluctantly signed them; he later failed to negotiate them in New York. Placed in command at St. Peter, he led poorly supplied troops, relieved Fort Ridgely, assembled about 2,000 men and a battery, reached Camp Release, secured surrender and captives' release, and formed a military tribunal for suspected offenders.

Pioneer Guards was a military company and organization, described as the oldest in the state and the finest in the West. Formed for Washington's birthday celebrations, it received Minie rifles and used Armory hall from 1859 until war began. Its annual ball was a leading social event; it soon disbanded, with members joining Union and Confederate forces.

called Minnesota legislature [into extra session to address the outbreak] Gov. Alexander Ramsey called an extra legislative session to arrange arms, equipment, and shelter for refugees. He also tried to calm St. Paul residents by stating that the nearest reported attacks were many miles from the capital.

The People's theater was an old frame theatrical building on the corner of Fourth and St. Peter streets, described as the only real theatrical building in St. Paul. H. Van Liew leased and managed it with a stock company including Emily Dow, Harry Gossan, and Azelene Allen. In summer 1858, J.W. Wallack and Mrs. J.W. Wallack appeared for two weeks, performing works including Macbeth and The Man in the Iron Mask; Mrs. Wallack portrayed Lady Macbeth. Col. R.E.J. Miles was a star and first produced Mazeppa there. A.M. Carver often performed, including as Uncle Tom in Uncle Tom's Cabin. Its gallery charged the shaded gentry parquet prices, and Joe Rolette sometimes had epileptic fits during performances.
James Buchanan exchanged messages with Queen Victoria after the successful laying of the Atlantic cable. In St. Paul's celebration, he was represented by George Folsom, a product of the city.

The Winslow telegraph line, reaching St. Paul, was completed in summer 1860. It ended newspapers’ heavy reliance on steamboats and mail coaches for distant news. Before it, the narrator met arriving boats at the levee by their whistles; afterward, high rates limited use, though the Pioneer secretly obtained service.

is_competed_for_by Pioneer [among St. Paul daily papers] The Pioneer, Minnesotian, and Times competed intensely to publish the full text of the president's message first. Printers prepared large staffs and distributed type in advance, while one Minnesotian proprietor unsuccessfully traveled to intercept an earlier copy.

depresses business [business of every description] The panic of 1857 had a very depressing effect on business. Supporters of the Five Million Loan measure argued that it would employ thousands and revive railroad building, land speculation, and other economic activity.

The Civil War began in 1861 and became a desperate conflict lasting more than four years. It placed severe demands on the United States government, contributing in 1862 to delayed Sioux annuity payments and limited readiness for the Sioux outbreak. St. Paul mobilized through patriotic meetings, enlistment appeals, and support for soldiers’ dependents; the Pioneer Guards disbanded, with many members becoming Union officers and two or three joining Confederate forces. Many printers and editors enlisted or served as officers in infantry, cavalry, artillery, sharpshooter, and other units, straining the Press’s staff as it supported vigorous prosecution of the war and faced hostility to the draft. By Lincoln’s assassination, Richmond had fallen, Lee had surrendered, and Johnston’s probable surrender appeared likely to end the war.

William H. Seward, Secretary of State and foremost statesman of his time, used diplomatic skill during the war to keep the United States free from foreign entanglements. Targeted in an assassination conspiracy and initially believed killed, he survived the dagger attack.
Earle S. Goodrich, a printer and Pioneer editor-in-chief, set the first type in the Press’s new building in 1869, composing editorial copy that began with an error.

l: First Battle of Bull Run, Novel-10146
s: is_a Union reverse [despite earlier reports of victory] Initial reports of the First Battle of Bull Run announced a Union victory, causing James M. Goodhue to feel confident after attending Dan Rice's circus. Later reports revealed a major Union reverse, and Gov. Marshall expressed deep concern about the country's prospects.

Abraham Lincoln was President of the United States during the Civil War, described as the greatest of all presidents, a martyred president, and an ideal statesman. In 1862 he issued a 600,000-volunteer enlistment, responded to the Minnesota draft, and limited condemned Indians’ executions to thirty-eight cases. He spoke of firmness for the right, led the country through more than four years of war, and was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth as Union victory appeared near.

Union forces, a military force under George H. Thomas, advanced in the Mill Springs campaign and defeated Confederate forces near Logan's Cross Roads, capturing cannon, wagons, ammunition, and supplies.
A draft was ordered in several Minnesota counties behind military quotas; despite bitter opposition and feared riot, fort troops were brought and it proceeded without interruption.

is_a holiday On July 4, 1863, the Pioneer was moving its plant, while the Press issued an extra containing news of Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg. The day became the occasion of St. Paul's greatest celebration up to that time.

occurred_during the Civil War [on July 4, 1863] The surrender of Vicksburg occurred on July 4, 1863, along with the battle of Gettysburg. News of it was reported in the Press's extra and helped prompt intense public excitement in St. Paul.

The American Civil War was an American civil conflict and a great crisis and struggle in which Minnesota volunteers served. It included early Union success at the Battle of Mill Springs and the exceptionally severe Battle of Pittsburg Landing, with consequences for Union commanders and operations. On July 4, 1863, the battle of Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg occurred. Later, fighting continued before Atlanta and in the march from Atlanta to the sea; enlistment also reduced volunteer fire departments, while daily newspapers expanded during the latter part of the war.

A narrator arrived in St. Paul on April 17, 1858, worked for the Daily Minnesotian, and in 1863 helped prepare Press news, distributed papers through a crowd, and sold them at the counting room window.

l: the Fourth of July celebration in St. Paul (1863), Novel-10146
s: celebrated Union victories [before sundown] The celebration followed the circulation of news about Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg. Cheers, cannon, anvils, firecrackers, and other noises filled the city, and before sundown St. Paul had celebrated what the narrator called the greatest Fourth of July in its history.

l: admission of Minnesota into the Union, Novel-10146
s: made_minnesota_part_of the Union [by an act of Congress] Congress passed a bill admitting Minnesota into the Union. The Pioneer published the news before the Minnesotian and Times, while the Minnesotian later issued an extra and sent it to subscribers.
The Union side in the American Civil War was defended by House of Hope members, supported by Noble’s sermons, and approached victory when Lincoln was assassinated.

l: Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company, Novel-10146
s: During the steamboat era, Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company operated steamers on the upper Mississippi, linking St. Louis, Dubuque, Prairie du Chien and La Crosse; arrivals drew people to St. Paul's levee.
The Fuller house was the former name of the International hotel. A.G. Fuller erected the five-story brick building in 1856, and it later became the International hotel under Samuel Mayall.

Winslow house was a four-story brick hotel at Seven Corners, constructed by J.M. Winslow in 1854 and among the city’s largest except Fuller house. In fall 1862, a defective cupola stovepipe caused a fire that entirely destroyed it; proprietors were arrested and discharged.
American house, a city landmark hotel at Third and Exchange streets, was built in 1849 and burned in 1863 before firefighters arrived; guests escaped, but thieves took jewelry and clothing.

Central house was a hotel at Bench and Minnesota streets, described as the first hotel of any pretension in St. Paul. Its dining room hosted the first territorial legislature session; later a boarding house, it burned in August 1873.

The Five Million Loan Election was a Minnesota constitutional amendment election authorizing state aid of $10,000 per mile to four railroad companies for road graded and ready to iron. Intended to promote railroad development and employment, it had leading bipartisan support and passed by an immense majority after the panic of 1857.

l: railroad companies receiving state bonds, Novel-10146
s: demand_bonds_from Henry H. Sibley [after work commenced] Four railroad companies were to receive $10,000 in state bonds for every mile of road graded and ready to iron. They demanded that Gov. Sibley issue the bonds, rejected his restrictions, obtained a peremptory writ from the supreme court, and later defaulted when the railroad construction scheme collapsed.

fail_to_be_negotiated_in New York [during Henry H. Sibley's attempt to market them] The Minnesota state bonds issued for railroad construction could not be negotiated in the New York market, compromising the state's credit. They were repudiated for more than twenty years before the state compromised with their holders and paid half their nominal value.

orders_issuance_of Minnesota state bonds [by peremptory writ] The Minnesota Supreme Court issued a peremptory writ directing Gov. Sibley to issue the railroad bonds. Judge Flandrau dissented, believing the state's financial reputation would have been greatly improved had his position prevailed.

Charles E. Flandrau dissented from the Minnesota Supreme Court bond opinion, organized volunteers at St. Peter during the 1862 Sioux outbreak, commanded New Ulm’s defense, and led its evacuation to Mankato when supplies ran short.

forecloses_on railroad development in Minnesota [nearly 250 miles of road were graded] The state of Minnesota faced a compromised credit after the railroad companies defaulted and the bonds could not be sold. It foreclosed on nearly 250 miles of graded railroad and later donated the lines to new organizations before settling with bondholders for 50 percent of the securities' nominal value.
Shakopee is a place near the late-May 1858 battle between Sioux and Chippewa warriors, where reporters stayed for days anticipating further engagements.

The Sioux occupied a strip along the Minnesota River and were hereditary enemies of the Chippewas. Divided between a government-favored farming party and an opposing Indian party, they had grievances over land, trader accounts, annuity deductions, and delayed payments, and communicated with Hole-in-the-Day. Before and during the 1862 outbreak, they attacked settlers, Company B, and fought at Fort Ridgely, New Ulm, Birch Coulie, and Wood Lake. Routed at Wood Lake, many at Camp Release were implicated in massacres, and the Sioux forfeited their Minnesota lands.

are_commanded_by Hole-in-the-day [during the Shakopee engagement] A party of Chippewa warriors under Chief Hole-in-the-day surprised Sioux near Shakopee and opened fire, killing or wounding fifteen or twenty. Eight or ten Chippewas were killed during the engagement.

The Atlantic cable was successfully laid in 1858, enabling messages between Great Britain and Queen Victoria and President Buchanan; it operated for about four weeks, ending with its last message on St. Paul's celebration.

l: celebration of the successful laying of the Atlantic cable, Novel-10146
s: takes_place_in St. Paul [on the first day of September 1858] St. Paul held an elaborate celebration on September 1, 1858, with a procession nearly two miles long, military units, floats, civic officials, secret societies, and thousands of spectators. Fireworks were postponed because of a storm, and the celebration coincided with the last message exchanged between England and America.
Queen Victoria exchanged messages with President Buchanan after the Atlantic cable was completed. Her representative in St. Paul's 1858 procession was Miss Rosa Larpenteur.

United States is a place where many cities organized bucket fire departments early in the nineteenth century; hand engines became common about fifty years later, and Cincinnati introduced the first paid steam fire department. Later, after President Abraham Lincoln’s assassination, it was plunged into mourning with draped buildings and church memorial services.

The St. Paul procession honoring the Atlantic cable, nearly two miles long and led by marshal-in-chief A.C. Jones, marched for three and one-half hours with diverse civic, military, religious, trade, and citizen participants to its destination.

l: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Novel-10146
s: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 was a volunteer fire company organized under the city charter in November 1854, whose members had to respond promptly to fire alarms. It included foreman Isaac A. Banker, officers, and members Washington M. Stees and Charles H. Williams, later chief and assistant chief engineers. In 1856 its accounts went to St. Paul and it owned fire equipment; it participated in an 1859 parade.

Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, organized in winter 1857-1858, was a prosperous engine company with Grant and O'Connor among its officers. Its engine house near Third and Jackson streets served members as a lounging and reading room, and it participated in the 1859 parade.

Hope Engine Company No. 1, organized in 1857, petitioned for hose and included foreman Michael Leroy with assistants R.C. Wiley and Joseph S. Herey. It received a double-deck hand engine in 1858, moved from Franklin and Fourth streets to Third street, and disbanded over the first steamer’s engineer.

Pioneer Press, a newspaper, absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861 and united with the Pioneer in 1874. By 1908, Frank Moore had served it and its antecedents for fifty years, heading its composing room; it employed George H. Colgrave.

succeeds_after_attempts four attempts [first in 1857, second in 1858, third in 1863, successful in 1865] The Atlantic cable enterprise required four attempts before success: in 1857, 1858, 1863, and 1865. The 1858 cable operated for about four weeks, while a new company laid a cable in 1866 that was in successful operation at the time described.
Cyrus W. Field projected the Atlantic cable enterprise, received unanimous thanks from Congress, and declined a knighthood Great Britain would have offered.

collapses suddenly The railroad construction scheme promised state bonds to companies for graded railroad mileage and was expected to revive employment and commerce after the panic of 1857. It collapsed when the bonds could not be negotiated, the companies defaulted, and the state's credit was compromised.

The Five Million Loan amendment encouraged railroad development in Minnesota by offering $10,000 per mile for road graded and ready to iron. Nearly 250 miles were graded before the state foreclosed on the lines and later donated them to new organizations.

Steamboat travel, historically used on the upper Mississippi, was the primary route there: pleasant in summer, but difficult and costly eastward in winter, forcing merchants to stock goods from November through April.

is_absent_from St. Paul [when the cable completion news arrived] St. Paul had no telegraphic communication when the Atlantic cable was completed, so news of the event arrived several days late. The city later celebrated after messages had been exchanged between Queen Victoria and President Buchanan.

The Sons of Malta were a secret order organized in the early 1850s that expanded rapidly throughout the West. After receiving a charter from Pittsburgh in 1858, Pioneer editorial staff established a successful St. Paul lodge at Empire Hall, drawing merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and many local men. Its elaborate, secret initiations investigated candidates and included confessions, frightening ceremonies, and rubber-blanket bouncing. Its membership and reputation declined after member Rev. John Penman exposed its secret work in Harper's Weekly.

The Minnesotian and Times was a consolidated newspaper, politically arranged from two rival Republican papers. Managed by Dr. Foster and Thomas M. Newson, it was marked by their uncordial relationship and ended when their partnership dissolved around the legislature’s adjournment.

St. Paul Press, also called the St. Paul Daily Press, was founded in 1861 by W. R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter using the Times office and material leased from Thomas M. Newson. Its competition led Dr. Foster to sell the Minnesotian plant, ending their rivalry. It employed foremen, moved in 1869, and united with Pioneer in 1874.

The Daily North Star was a short-lived Democratic newspaper established in St. Paul during the 1860 presidential campaign to support John C. Breckinridge. H. H. Young was brought to start it. It published regularly through the election, then collapsed when officeholders no longer contributed support.

is_selected_by legislature [after the 1859 election] The office of state printer became the subject of a vigorous contest after the Republican victory in 1859. The Minnesotian and Times both sought the position, while Orville Brown of Faribault entered the race and nearly secured the legislative printing for that village. George W. Moore received the printing of the journals of the two legislative houses as part of the settlement of the former newspaper partnership.

is_exposed_in Harper’s Weekly [with numerous illustrations] The Sons of Malta's secret initiation involved hooded candidates being questioned about their conduct before the full lodge, despite believing they were in a private chamber. The ceremony included frightening sounds, public humiliation, and other physical ordeals, including bouncing candidates from a rubber blanket. Rev. John Penman's anger over his treatment led him to publish an illustrated exposure of the secret work.

l: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862, Novel-10146
s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 was Indian warfare in western Minnesota during the Civil War. Beginning without warning on August 18, it caused a Sioux massacre across the reservation, spread rapidly, killed people, destroyed property, and rendered 30,000 homeless within a week. After the Wood Lake battle, Gen. Pope declared the war over; troops remained despite calls to remove them.

In 1862, during the Civil War, the United States government was heavily occupied and considered unprepared for the Sioux outbreak. It delayed Sioux annuity payments, though its officers promoted farming, supplied tools and seed, and built houses for some Sioux. After events at Sumter, St. Paul citizens pledged it earnest support, urging enlistment and aid for servicemen’s families.
The Confederate States adopted "Dixie" as their national air after it became popular in New Orleans and throughout the South during the Civil War.

Ulysses S. Grant commanded Union forces at Pittsburg Landing, directing divisions despite an injured ankle, stopping a flight, and leading the second-day pursuit. His Fort Henry and Fort Donelson successes made superiors jealous. Afterward he became second to Henry W. Halleck, who succeeded him, and was reassigned to Memphis.

Don Carlos Buell commanded the Army of the Cumberland and was criticized for taking nineteen days to move approximately eighty-five miles to the Tennessee River. His troops, including divisions under Nelson and Thomas, reinforced Grant during the battle; Grant did not believe Buell was guilty of the charges later made against him.

Little Crow was born at Kaposia and influenced the 1858 sale of part of the Minnesota River reservation strip, drawing Sioux criticism. He became the acknowledged head of the war party and was described as chief instigator of the insurrection. After refusing surrender at Camp Release, he escaped, was killed by Lamson near Hutchinson, and his scalp was preserved by the Minnesota Historical Society.

Other Day, an educated Dakota Indian who adopted Christianity and civilized habits, guided sixty-two Minnesota River refugees through several places to safety. After arriving in St. Paul, he credited the Great Spirit for their escape and supported Gen. Sibley by fighting with the whites.

Constructed in 1860 on Bridge Square, Ingersoll block was a city block whose third-floor hall drew audiences for several years. It hosted speakers Edward Everett, Ralph Waldo Emerson, John B. Gough, and Mrs. Scott Siddons; Company C used it for drills and enlistment meetings. In February 1861, a Young Men's Christian Association social and supper raised library funds for about 350 books.

Fort Ridgely was a lightly protected post besieged during the Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 by an estimated 700 or 800 Sioux warriors. About 150 Fifth Regiment men, fifty Renville Rangers, and civilians defended it for more than a week until relief arrived with the advance of Sibley’s force.

was_attacked_by Sioux [repeatedly, with burning and pillaging] New Ulm was attacked by Sioux forces that killed citizens and burned buildings. After a later attack, its defenders evacuated about 1,200 to 1,500 noncombatants to Mankato, and nearly 200 houses had been burned.
Mankato held the condemned Indians in a large jail before the authorized executions. Thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were executed there on December 26, 1862.

Birch Coulie was the site of a camp established by Maj. Joseph R. Brown’s detachment about fifteen miles from Fort Ridgely. The camp’s attractive but exposed location left roughly 150 men vulnerable to a large Sioux attack.

Battle of Wood Lake, the Indian war's only real battle, occurred at Wood Lake on September 23. About 800 of Gen. Sibley's men fought roughly 800 Sioux; Col. Marshall's 400-man charge routed them, with four whites killed and forty or fifty wounded.
Wood Lake was the vicinity where foraging parties from the Third regiment were fired upon on the morning of September 23, 1862.

The Birch Coulie battle began around 4 a.m. when 500 or 600 armed, mostly mounted Sioux fired on Maj. Joseph R. Brown’s roughly 150-man command. The defenders held out for two days until relief arrived, with about half killed or wounded.

The Sioux massacre began on August 18 with attacks on settlers and spread throughout the reservation and isolated communities. The text reports that about 1,000 people were killed in less than a week, millions of dollars in property were destroyed, and 30,000 people were made homeless.

The Fort Ridgely siege lasted several days and included two attempted assaults by Sioux forces. Defenders improvised ammunition by opening spherical case shot, making cartridges, and cutting nail rods into projectiles until relief arrived.

The New Ulm attacks included an initial assault that killed citizens and burned homes, followed several days later by a larger encirclement and assault. Flandrau’s defenders drove the Sioux away, but lost ten men killed and about forty wounded before evacuating the town.
Gen. Sibley's command reached Camp Release on September 26, where a large Indian camp surrendered after preliminary consultations. The captives held there were released.

l: Indian camp at Camp Release, Novel-10146
s: contains mixed bloods and white women and children [about 250 captives] The Indian camp at Camp Release contained many Indians who had participated in the massacres and held about 250 mixed bloods and white women and children. The entire camp surrendered after Gen. Sibley avoided a hostile demonstration that he believed might lead to the prisoners' annihilation.

l: mixed bloods and white women and children, Novel-10146
s: are_released_at Camp Release [after the entire camp surrendered] About 250 mixed bloods and white women and children were held by the Indian camp at Camp Release. They were released when the camp surrendered.

convicts condemned Indians [321 defendants found guilty] Gen. Sibley formed a military tribunal to investigate and try Indians suspected of participating in the recent atrocities. After sittings from September 30 to November 5, it found 321 guilty, sentencing 303 to death and the remainder to imprisonment.

The condemned Indians were taken to Mankato and confined in a specially constructed jail; after executions were reduced to thirty-eight, the remaining prisoners stayed until spring and were transported to Davenport and the Missouri river.

l: execution of the thirty-eight Dakota prisoners, Novel-10146
s: occurs_at Mankato [on December 26, 1862] The thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were hanged at Mankato on December 26, 1862. Their bodies were placed together in a sandbar grave and were later taken away by students and others familiar with dissection.

uses wagon [because there were no railroads] Because there were no railroads, military supplies had to be transported by wagon. The authorities impressed teams into government service when volunteers were insufficient, sent Company K of the Eighth regiment to enforce the order, and provided escorts for supply trains.

Ladies Aid Society in St. Paul organized to sew and provide supplies for wounded soldiers and destitute refugees, meeting at Ingersoll Hall; Stella Selby led it and M.O. Holyoke collected sanitary supplies.
Dakota lands in Minnesota, about 750,000 acres valued at $15,000,000, are forfeited to the government following the outbreak, along with a $68,000 annual annuity for fifty years.

The St. Paul Fire Department developed from volunteer companies organized in the 1850s, including Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. It held its first annual parade in 1859. By March 1860 it had three fire engines, one fire truck, and one hundred men. After its first steamer arrived August 11, 1866, it expanded despite the city’s lack of waterworks in 1869, relying on cisterns and river water pumped through over two thousand feet of hose. At present it has 211 paid men, 15 steamers, four chemicals, eight hook and ladder companies, and 122 horses; chiefs include Wash M. Stees and Bartlett Presley.

l: firemen and fires of pioneer days, Novel-10146
s: is_a brief history The unit describes pioneer firemen responding to alarms with hand engines, hooks, ladders, and bucket brigades. Firemen worked the engine brakes, sometimes requiring spectators or people compelled by the police to relieve them, and many enlisted during the war.

is_used_by old firemen [in the poem's recollection] The old machine is remembered in a poem by Gus Wiliams as a former fire apparatus with which firemen ran through flames and danger. The poem says that only a few of the old firemen remained, while their memories and spirits endured.

is_a firefighting equipment Early fire engines included wheeled tanks, hand engines, and engines equipped with pumps, air chambers, suction pipes, and leather hose. St. Paul received its first engine through John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie and later purchased two double-deck hand engines that arrived in August 1858.
R.C. Knox first tried to organize a St. Paul fire brigade in fall 1851, raised subscription money for ladders, and was reputed to outlast a dozen ordinary men at fires.

John McCloud, a hardware dealer and member of McCloud & Bro., jointly bought and brought the first fire engine introduced in the Northwest to St. Paul with Thompson Ritchie. He was an original member and the only surviving city resident of Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1's original roll.

l: first parade of the St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146
s: The first parade of the St. Paul fire department took place September 12, 1859, with 175 men from Pioneer Hook and Ladder, Hope Engine, Minnehaha Engine, and Rotary Independent companies participating.
The first steamer arrived in St. Paul on August 11, 1866, was initially housed by Hope Engine Company No. 1 with appointed staff, then transferred to St. Paul Hose Company No. 1 after disbandment.

Mrs. Bartlett Presley supports the volunteer fire department as a guardian angel, attending fires during cold nights and severe storms to provide coffee and sandwiches, earning firemen’s lasting gratitude.
Michael E. Ames, a St. Paul legal fraternity member living in uppertown, escaped a fire that destroyed his sleeping apartments after asking firemen to wait.

l: St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859, Novel-10146
s: The St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859 was held on September 12 and included four companies. The 175 participants completed a line of march and were reviewed by the mayor and common council in front of the old city hall.

replaces volunteer fire department [after the volunteer era] The paid fire department followed the volunteer period and expanded as St. Paul grew. At the time described, it had 211 paid men, 15 steamers, 4 chemicals, 8 hook and ladder companies, and 122 horses.

The volunteer fire department was organized through companies such as Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. Its members received exemptions from jury duty, poll tax, road work, and state military service for five years, and many prominent citizens served in its ranks.

Firefighting equipment discussed in the unit includes marked buckets, ladders, hooks, hand engines, hose, cisterns, steamers, chemical apparatus, and horses. St. Paul initially had limited equipment, then acquired two double-deck hand engines in 1858 and additional apparatus as the city expanded.

is_a list of hotels destroyed by fire [during St. Paul's early history] The unit lists hotels destroyed by fire during St. Paul’s early history, including the Daniels house, Sintominie hotel, Rice house, New England hotel, Winslow house, American house, International hotel, Cosmopolitan hotel, Central house, Emmert house, Greenman house, Mansion house, Park Place hotel, and Carpenter house.

Daniels house was a hotel on Eagle street near Seven Corners, finished and furnished shortly before strong wind hindered firemen and it was destroyed in the 1852 Daniels house fire; furniture was partly saved.
Hotel at Sixth and John streets, constructed by C.W. Borup; Howard Ward and E.C. Rich prepared to open it before the Sintominie hotel fire totally destroyed it.

Rice house was a three-story hotel on Third street near Market, built by Henry M. Rice and commonly considered St. Paul’s first brick building. A principal hotel, it hosted Minnesota’s territorial legislature and the territory’s supreme court before burning to the ground in early winter 1856.

New England hotel was a two-story log house in St. Paul, among its first hotels. Gov. and Mrs. Ramsey lived there in 1849, giving it recognition as the first gubernatorial mansion, before the March 16, 1860 fire destroyed it.

The International hotel, formerly the Fuller house, was a five-story brick building at Seventh and Jackson streets, built by A.G. Fuller in 1856 for about $110,000. Renamed in 1861 and once regarded as the best hotel in the West, it burned in the February 3, 1869 fire.

The Cosmopolitan hotel, a European-plan hotel in a three-story brick building at Third and Franklin streets, was remodeled from a former banking house by Bechtner & Kottman, then burned while full of lodgers; many lost everything, and its remaining walls collapsed onto Dr. Schell’s building.

The Emmert house was a hotel and later boarding house on Bench street near Wabasha, built in territorial times by Fred Emmert. No longer a hotel, it housed a family and boarders when fire destroyed it in winter 1868; firemen rescued two people sick with smallpox, and W.L. Wilson took them to safety.

Greenman house was a three-story frame building at Fifth and St. Peter streets, built in the early 1870s. Mr. Greenman sold it to John Summers; while Summers owned it, the Greenman house fire destroyed it.

The Mansion house was a three-story frame hotel built by Nicholas Pottgieser for $12,000 at Wabasha and Fifth streets, a popular resort where, in 1866, guest Hawkes accidentally killed his wife and was acquitted.

Park Place hotel was a four-story frame family hotel at Summit avenue and St. Peter street, formerly fashionable but unoccupied when it burned to the ground on May 19, 1878. The suspected incendiary fire seriously injured four firemen, who recovered.

Carpenter house was a hotel at Summit avenue and Ramsey street, built by Warren Carpenter on a picturesque site overlooking the city to attract tourists. The panic of 1857 and Civil war thwarted plans; it later burned to the ground January 26, 1879.

is_a hotel fire [the first hotel fire of any importance] The 1852 Daniels house fire was the first hotel fire of importance described in the unit. A strong wind prevented the small group of firemen from saving the newly finished building, though furniture was rescued.

The March 16, 1860 St. Paul fire began in a small wooden building on Third street near Jackson, became the city’s most destructive fire to that time, burned thirty-four buildings including two hotels, and was stopped from crossing Robert street into lower town.

The Winslow house fire occurred in the fall of 1862 and was caused by a defective stovepipe in the cupola. The four-story brick hotel was beyond control when firemen arrived, and only a few badly damaged pieces of furniture were saved.

The Cosmopolitan hotel fire destroyed a hotel full of lodgers, many of whom lost all they owned. The walls remained standing afterward despite being declared dangerous, and a later collapse crushed Dr. Schell’s nearby frame building, though he survived with no serious injury.

The Emmert house fire occurred during the winter of 1868. Two occupants suffering from smallpox were rescued by firemen but were left in the street until W.L. Wilson learned of their situation the next day and took them to safety.

The February 3, 1869 International hotel fire began in the basement, probably from a laundry lamp, on a cold, gale-driven night. Pete O’Brien helped more than two hundred guests escape; no lives were lost, but the hotel and four other buildings were destroyed.

The May 1870 Concert Hall fire began beneath the sidewalk, where combustible materials were stored, and rapidly engulfed the building. Charles and August Mueller leaped from an upper-floor window and survived after months of suffering, while McClellan, who operated a dressmaking establishment there, was burned to death.

St. Paul Concert Hall was a concert hall in a three-story building on Third street near Market, with six or seven stories on the river side and a large basement hall. Built by J.W. McClung in 1857, it held about 400 or 500 people. Its basement location made it somewhat inaccessible and limited demand, yet it hosted speeches and musical gatherings. It was destroyed in the May 1870 Concert Hall fire.

The Athenaeum, built in 1859 by the German Reading Society, was for several years St. Paul's only amusement hall with a stage and drop curtain. It hosted Peter and Caroline Richings, dramatic performances, and a Sanitary Commission benefit; during the Sioux massacre, it sheltered maimed refugees.

Firemen fought numerous St. Paul fires despite strong winds, bitter cold, limited equipment, and a lack of waterworks. They saved furniture at the Daniels house, rescued guests and smallpox patients, and at the International hotel were aided by the calm direction of Pete O’Brien.

Hotel guests faced narrow escapes during several fires. At the American house they escaped in bitter cold while thieves stole their belongings, and at the International hotel more than two hundred guests fled in nightclothes without any lives being lost.

The unit describes fires caused or suspected to have been caused by strong winds, defective stovepipes, lamps, and possible incendiarism. Fires destroyed hotels and other buildings, threatened entire sections of St. Paul, and sometimes required rescues from severe cold, smoke, flames, or collapsing walls.

Irvine hall was an amusement hall in a three-story, three-cornered building on Third street at Seven Corners. Later called Melodeon hall, it hosted Dan Emmet's minstrel company in 1857–1858 and the Hutchinson family in summer 1858.

Dan Emmet was a minstrel performer who organized the first traveling minstrel troupe in the United States in 1843. He later led a company at Irvine hall in 1857–1858 and wrote popular melodies, including "Dixie," while connected with Bryant's Minstrels.

The Hutchinson family was a patriotic concert-giving family that generally sang its own music. It frequently visited St. Paul, and Hutchinson in McLeod county was named after it. During the Civil War, Gen. McClellan removed it from the Army of the Potomac for abolitionist songs. In 1902, John W. Hutchinson was identified as its last surviving member.
R.C. Munger was Dan Emmet’s friend in St. Paul, encouraged and financed publication of “Dixie,” received an early printed copy, and saw it first sung in the West at Munger Bros.’ music store.

Dixie, an air written by Dan Emmet with Bryant's Minstrels in New York City, was first sung west at Munger Bros, spread through minstrel programs, became the Confederate States' national air, and Lincoln called it national property by capture.

receives_funds_from sanitary fair [several thousand dollars from St. Paul citizens] The sanitary commission received several thousand dollars from the successful 1864 sanitary fair in St. Paul. The fair was part of a broader practice of holding fairs in principal Northern cities to raise money for the commission.

Market Hall, built in 1853 at Wabasha and Seventh streets, became one of St. Paul’s principal places of amusement, hosting the Hough Dramatic Company before serving the Wide Awakes as a drill hall in 1860.

William Henry Acker, born in New York State in 1833, came to St. Paul in 1854 and became a respected military leader. He was captain of the Pioneer Guards, commanded the Wide-Awakes in 1860, and, at the war’s outbreak, served as Minnesota’s adjutant general and organized a company for the First Minnesota Regiment. Wounded at Bull Run, he became captain in the Seventeenth United States Regulars. He was killed leading his company at Pittsburg Landing; his funeral was at St. Paul’s Church, and Acker Post was named for him.

Mazurka hall was the principal amusement hall of the city for a time. Built by the Elfelt brothers in 1850, it occupied the second story of their old frame building at Third and Exchange streets. It hosted swell entertainments in the early 1850s, including a ball where J.Q.A. Ward met and soon married Miss Pratt.
