Mozart hall, the People’s theater, was an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St., built by Charles N. Mackubin in 1860 at the Third Street end of the Metropolitan hotel site; it joined Masonic hall for a winter 1864 sanitary fair.

Masonic hall, an old frame building on the Fourth Street corner of the Metropolitan hotel site, was built by Charles N. Mackubin in summer 1860 and joined with Mozart hall for a large sanitary-fair entertainment in winter 1864.

benefits sanitary commission [held during the winter of 1864] A sanitary fair held in the winter of 1864 combined Mozart hall and Masonic hall for a large entertainment. Its proceeds helped the nearly depleted funds of the sanitary commission, and the event raised several thousand dollars.

The Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment was a Union infantry regiment from Minnesota, organized in 1861 under Colonel H.P. Van Cleve and headquartered at Fort Snelling. It moved toward Washington, was redirected to Louisville, reported to W.T. Sherman, and joined George H. Thomas's First Division. In the Mill Springs campaign, it camped at Logan's Cross Roads, fought in the center under heavy fire, used bayonets, lost twelve killed and thirty-five wounded, received praise, and was presented a silk flag.

Adalina Patti was a concert performer, about sixteen in 1857. That year, on her first appearance in St. Paul, she traveled with the Ole Bull Concert company by small steamboat through river towns and performed in the old capitol’s house of representatives hall.

contains house of representatives [the hall served as a concert venue] The old capitol provided the only available venue for Adalina Patti's 1857 concert. Two boys who had been using the house for smoking and playing cards accidentally caused a fire that nearly burned through its floor.

The hall of the house of representatives hosted Adalina Patti's 1857 concert, Washington's Birthday exercises, a mass meeting supporting the government after the attack on Sumter, and the first Republican state convention after Minnesota entered the Union. The hall was also the scene of speeches, resolutions, and political nominations.

After Maj. Anderson was compelled to lower the Stars and Stripes on Sumter's walls, St. Paul citizens held a mass meeting to express indignation at the attempt of the Cotton States to disrupt the government. The meeting pledged support to the government, urged young men to enlist, and promised financial aid for dependents of those who served.
John S. Prince, mayor of St. Paul, presided over the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. He was assisted by several prominent citizens serving as vice presidents.

John M. Gilman was one of the principal speakers at the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. Although he had been the Democratic candidate for Congress the previous fall, he expressed hearty sympathy with the meeting's support for the government and received strong approval.

Confederate forces were a military force commanded overall by Albert Sidney Johnston and also by P. G. T. Beauregard. They held Beech Grove, advanced near Logan's Cross Roads, and were driven off with about 600 casualties. They later attacked Grant's army, failed to destroy it or stop a counterattack, and retreated toward Corinth.

The old opera house on Wabasha Street, on the ground now occupied by the Grand block, was completed in winter 1866–67 and opened with local talent. Its boxes and some parquet seats were auctioned; Macfarland Dramatic Company became its first regular company. Seating about 1,000, it later drew large audiences for Frederick Douglass and other speakers.

addresses_audience_at old opera house [during a lecture with standing room only] Frederick Douglass addressed a large audience at the old opera house in St. Paul. During his lecture, two Republicans in an upper box applauded loudly while standing behind W.H. Shelley, causing the audience to think Shelley was supporting Douglass and had returned to the Republican fold; Shelley eventually left in disgust.

Capt. E.Y. Shelly was a pioneer printer of Minnesota, born in Bucks county, Pa., in 1827 and trained in Philadelphia. After service in the Third United States dragoons during the Mexican War, he reached St. Paul in July 1849 as Minnesota’s first permanent printer. He worked for the Register, Pioneer, and Daily Democrat, served in Brackett’s battalion during the Civil War, was mustered out in 1865, and continued printing afterward.
George W. Benedict, familiar to longtime residents, served as foreman of the St. Paul Press before becoming editor and publisher of the Sauk Rapids Sentinel.

Louis E. Fisher was a printer, foreman of the Commercial Advertiser, and longtime editor of the Pioneer and Pioneer Press. A staunch Democrat, he ran unsuccessfully for governor of Minnesota and was described as a potential model governor.

George W. Armstrong, known as the Beau Brummel of early territorial printers for wearing kid gloves while making up forms at the Pioneer, was elected state treasurer on the Democratic ticket in 1857 and later entered real estate.
David Ramaley, a leading Northwest printer, spent nearly fifty years as printer, reporter, editor, publisher, and type founder, remaining active throughout his long trade career.
James M. Culver was a fastidious printer, St. Paul’s first delegate to the International Typographical Union, and remembered by Sons of Malta for resisting a ceremony’s canine portion.

William Jebb, a ready, fluent, well-informed debater in the Pioneer composing room and former St. Paul Times reporter, left reporting after writing about stolen prized chickens and ending the report with a papal bull of excommunication.

O.G. Miller was a well-known, musically inclined St. Paul printer who belonged to the Great Western band, sang tenor in churches, and was a 33d Degree Mason; after his death, Masonic hall held a midnight funeral service.

Andrew Jackson Morgan was a printer-politician brought to St. Paul by Col. D.A. Robertson, who made him foreman of the Democrat; he later edited it. He claimed to resemble Stephen A. Douglas and carried a silver dollar reportedly given by Andrew Jackson at his christening. He died in Ohio.

P. G. T. Beauregard served with Albert Sidney Johnston as a Confederate commander at Pittsburg Landing. He reportedly said that before sundown he would water his horses in the Tennessee River or in hell, and later reported Confederate losses of 10,699.
